3.note: The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Bath Shua the Canaanitess bore three sons to him]

The author is using **in the eyes of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the judgment of]

6.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “Dara.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “Darda,” as in 1 Kings 4:31. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

7.note: The author assumes that readers will know that **Carmi** was the son of Zimri, whom he names in the previous verse. (Zimri is called Zabdi in Joshua 7:1.) You could indicate this in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Carmi, the son of Zimri]

Some ancient manuscripts read “Achar.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “Achan,” as in Joshua 7:1. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of how the author and characters often use the name of a nation to represent its people. Alternate translation: [the troubler of the Israelites] or [the man who caused trouble for the Israelites]

The word that the ULT translates as **devoted** is a specialized term that describes the cultural practice of giving something over to Yahweh so that humans will no longer be able to use it, often by destroying it completely. This is a reference to Joshua 7, which describes how Achar (who is called Achan there) took plunder from the city of Jericho even though Yahweh had forbidden the Israelites to do that. If you have already translated the book of Joshua, see how you represented the term “devoted” there. Alternate translation: [who sinned by taking things that Yahweh had forbidden the Israelites to take]

9.note: The author assumes that readers will know that the name **Chelubai** is a variant of Caleb. He describes this same man by the Caleb in verses 18–19, 24, and 42–50. You could also use the name Caleb here if that would be helpful to your readers. Decide as a translation team whether you will use the same name for a given person in each place where he appears or whether you will use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [Caleb]

10.note: The author is speaking as if the people of the tribe of Judah were actually the **sons** of Judah. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Judah]

11.note: The name **Salma** occurs here in the standard Hebrew text. You may want to use the name Salmon, which occurs here in the ancient Greek translation and in the Hebrew text in Ruth 4:20–21. The Greek text of Matthew 1:4–5 also reads “Salmon.” Alternate translation: [Salmon]

13.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second** or **third**, you could represent these numbers, as well as the similar numbers in the next two verses, in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [and Abinadab, son number two, and Shimea, son number three]

18.note: The pronoun **her** refers to **Azubah**. She is identified as a full **wife**, whose sons would have inheritance rights, by apparent contrast with **Jerioth**, who seems to have been a concubine. So the author names the sons of Azubah but not the sons of Jerioth. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And these were Azubah’s sons]

21.note: The author is referring to sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **went in to**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [Hezron slept with the daughter of Makir]

The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he had taken** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to indicate that he is speaking of **Hezron**, not **Makir** or **Gilead**. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Now Hezron had taken her]

In this culture, to say how old a man was, speakers would say that he was **a son of** a certain number of **years**. In your translation, express this in the way your language and culture say how old someone is. Alternate translation: [was 60 years of age]

23.note: The author is speaking as if the villages around **Kenath** were actually the **daughters** of that city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the surrounding villages]

24.q: וְ⁠אַחַ֥ר מוֹת־חֶצְר֖וֹן בְּ⁠כָלֵ֣ב אֶפְרָ֑תָה וְ⁠אֵ֤שֶׁת חֶצְרוֹן֙ אֲבִיָּ֔ה וַ⁠תֵּ֣לֶד ל֔⁠וֹ אֶת־אַשְׁח֖וּר אֲבִ֥י תְקֽוֹעַ
24.note: In this verse, the ULT presents a a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek translation. (That reading uses the name Ephrathah for the woman who is called Ephrath in 2:19.) Alternate translation: [After the death of Hezron, Caleb went in to Ephrathah, the widow of his father Hezron. And she bore to him Ashhur, the father of Tekoa]

42.note: This phrase is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading that many interpreters favor based on the likelihood that a word was left out at some point by copyists. Alternate translation: [And his second son Mareshah was the father of Hebron] or [And his next son Mareshah was the father of Hebron]

55.note: The author is using the term **father** to mean “ancestor.” He is using the term **house** to mean all the people descended from a particular person. The term envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Rechab** means all the people descended from Rechab. Alternate translation, as in the UST: [the ancestor of the Rechabites]
